deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the closing page (p.30; p.31 carries the struck-out signature 'Göttingen 14. Jan. 1847, B.R.') of Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation'. It was published posthumously in the Werke (1876). Notation: ∂^ν is the derivative of arbitrary order ν (negative ν means integration of order −ν). Π(s)=Γ(s+1) and Ψ(s)=dlogΠ(s)/ds=ψ(s+1) (digamma shifted). φ_ν is the 'complementary function', i.e. the undetermined part.

(a) Closing remark on 11/12. The values given by 11/12 for different ν 'correspond': they are mutually consistent under the composition law ∂^ν∂^μ=∂^{ν+μ}. This is the reason why, in 12, the term proportional to x^{μ−ν} (the term with Ψ(μ−ν)−Ψ_0) cannot simply be absorbed into the complementary function φ_ν. That term is fixed once one requires consistency across ν.

(b) Formula 13, e^x. Use the integral definition with lower limit −∞ (Liouville's choice):
∂^ν e^x = (1/Π(−ν−1)) ∫_{−∞}^x e^t (x−t)^{−ν−1} dt.
Substitute y=x−t (dt=−dy; t=−∞→y=∞, t=x→y=0) [step made explicit by me]:
= (1/Π(−ν−1)) e^x ∫_0^∞ e^{−y} y^{−ν−1} dy
= e^x Γ(−ν)/Π(−ν−1) = e^x.
The integral converges for ν<0. For ν≥0 the result follows by ordinary differentiation (his rules 7–10).

(c) Formula 14, log x. Riemann remarks this follows by the same method, but more easily and immediately for all ν from 6 (the composition law) and 12. Since d/dx log x = x^{−1}, we have ∂^ν log x = ∂^{ν−1}(x^{−1}). Apply 12 with μ=−1 and order ν−1. The prefactor Π(μ)/Π(−1) equals 1 and Π(μ−(ν−1)) = Π(−ν), so
∂^ν log x = (1/Π(−ν)) (log x · x^{−ν} ± [Ψ(−ν)−Ψ(0)] x^{−ν}).
The manuscript writes '+' in front of the bracket.

(d) Final remark. Rules 7–10 together with 13 and 14 give 'with the greatest ease' the derivatives of sin x, cos x, tg x and arctan x. Presumably this goes via sin and cos as combinations of e^{±ix} and via d/dx arctan x = 1/(1+x^2) [my interpretation]. The next page adds that the theory extends equally to imaginary values.
errors: Formula 13: there is no error. One caveat is that the integral representation holds only for ν<0 (Re ν<0); positive orders must be reached through the differentiation rules. The manuscript shows corrections in the integrand (x±t, dk→dt) and in the limits, but the final reading (x−t), limits −∞..x and 0..∞ is correct.

Formula 14 has a sign problem. With the standard Riemann–Liouville integral from 0, I^α log x = x^α/Γ(α+1)·(log x + ψ(1) − ψ(α+1)). With ν=−α this gives ∂^ν log x = x^{−ν}/Π(−ν)·(log x − [Ψ(−ν)−Ψ(0)]).
The '+' written in 14 fails the check ν=1. As ν→1, Ψ(−ν)/Π(−ν)→−1, so Riemann's '+' gives −1/x instead of 1/x. The '−' sign gives the correct 1/x.

The source of the sign error is the previous page. There ∫_0^1 (y^s−1)/(1−y) dy = −(Ψ(s)−Ψ(0)), and Riemann wrote '±' next to 'besondere Fehler[?]', showing he was unsure of the sign. The constant term cannot be dismissed as part of the complementary function, because on this very page he argues it is fixed by consistency across ν.
Minor: the claim that sin, cos, tan and arctan follow 'with the greatest ease' is only sketched. For tan x in particular, a closed form of arbitrary order is not easy.

results.what: ∂^ν e^x = e^x via the integral from −∞ and the substitution y=x−t, reducing to Euler's Gamma integral
results.modern_name: Liouville (Weyl-type, lower limit −∞) fractional derivative of the exponential
results.usually_credited_to: Liouville (1832); later Weyl (1917) for the −∞ base point

results.what: Fractional derivative/integral of log x of arbitrary order, expressed with Π (Gamma) and Ψ (digamma), obtained via ∂^ν log x = ∂^{ν−1} x^{−1}
results.modern_name: Riemann–Liouville fractional integral of the logarithm: I^α log x = x^α/Γ(α+1)(log x − γ − ψ(α+1))
results.usually_credited_to: Liouville (1830s) for log-type cases; standard in Riemann–Liouville calculus (e.g. Oldham–Spanier tables)

results.what: Remark that the x^{μ−ν} term for negative integer μ cannot be put into the complementary function because the values must be consistent under composition across ν
results.modern_name: Semigroup/index law consistency and the complementary function in Riemann's fractional calculus

deep.surprise_reason: This is the final page of Riemann's 1847 student essay on fractional differentiation. The essay was published in the Werke (1876) and is the origin of the name 'Riemann–Liouville'. The content (e^x invariance, the log formula, and the extension to trigonometric functions) is well known and largely follows Liouville. The only item of interest is a sign slip in formula 14.

checkable.asserts: Formula 13 for a sample ν<0: the substituted integral divided by Π(−ν−1)=Γ(−ν) gives e^x (result 0).
Riemann–Liouville integral of order a of log t from 0, evaluated at x=1, equals (log x + ψ(1) − ψ(a+1))/Γ(a+1); difference should be 0 numerically.
With the minus sign the formula for ∂^ν log x reduces to 1/x at ν=1. With Riemann's '+' it would give −1/x.
∫_0^1 (y^s−1)/(1−y) dy = −(Ψ(s)−Ψ(0)) with Ψ(s)=ψ(s+1); this is the source of the ± sign issue (result 0 at s=2).
At ν=0 formula 14 returns log x.

transcription_corrections: In formula 13 the struck-out leading symbol is a 'D^ν e^x' overwritten by ∂^ν e^x. The integrand shows corrections from (x±t)/(x+t) to (x−t), and 'dk' is corrected to dt. The lower limit −∞ is written over an earlier limit, and the second integral's limits 0..∞ are also written over earlier text.
In the margin at 14 the struck-out red symbols are 𝔇 forms, with ∂_x^ν and ∂_x^ν ∂_x^{−1} written beneath. The transcription's rendering is essentially right.
In formula 14 the bracket reads [Ψ(−ν) − Ψ(0)]; the image has 'Ψ(o)', i.e. Ψ(0). The sign before the bracket appears as '+'. Mathematically it should be '−' (see errors).

The word 'einschlossen' in line 4 is more likely 'einschliessen' or 'einschlossen' (subjunctive sense: 'could include'). The phrase 'für den Fall μ = einer negativen ganzen Zahl' may be a slip for the non-integer case, given formula 11 versus 12; the reading of the image is uncertain.
